meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's life that matters, nothing but life — the process of discovering, the everlasting process'?
meta.ogDescription: Real, and traceable to page 328 — but it is a character speaking, and this short form stops before the end of Garnett's sentence.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and locatable to the page: it appears in The Idiot, Part III, Chapter V, where the consumptive teenager Ippolit Terentyev reads it aloud from a manuscript Garnett titles “An Essential Explanation.” The memorable English is Constance Garnett’s 1913 translation, and her sentence runs on past the point where this shortened form stops.

source.heading: The Idiot, Part III, Chapter V

docMeta.dd: Part III, Chapter V — from Ippolit Terentyev’s “An Essential Explanation”
Constance Garnett, first published 1913; verified in the William Heinemann printing, London, 1918, p. 328

source.excerpt:
Ask them, ask them what they all, every one of them understand by happiness. Oh, you may be sure that Columbus was happy not when he had discovered America, but when he was discovering it. Take my word for it, the highest moment of his happiness was just three days before the discovery of the New World, when the mutinous crew were on the point of returning to Europe in despair. It wasn’t the New World that mattered, even if it had fallen to pieces.

Columbus died almost without seeing it; and not really knowing what he had discovered. It’s life that matters, nothing but life—the process of discovering, the everlasting and perpetual process, not the discovery itself, at all.
trail: Wikiquote’s Dostoyevsky page ↗ carries the line in its sourced material for The Idiot (1868–9), citing Part 3, Chapter 5, tr. Constance Garnett, 1913 — not among misattributed or disputed lines.

We then read the sentence in the translation itself. The Garnett text printed by William Heinemann in 1918 ↗ carries it word for word on page 328, inside the chapter where Ippolit reads his manuscript aloud.
The novel was serialised in The Russian Messenger across 1868–1869 ↗, and Garnett’s English Idiot is dated 1913 ↗.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation ↗, so there is no competing origin claim to weigh against the primary text.

author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.heading: The novelist behind the line
author.bio: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky spent four years in a Siberian prison camp after a mock execution in 1849, and the rest of his life writing novels in which people argue about God, suffering and free will at enormous length and terrible speed. The Idiot (1868–1869) was his attempt to put a genuinely good man — the epileptic Prince Myshkin — into Petersburg society and watch what happened. He almost never speaks in his own voice in the novels: the most quotable lines belong to characters he is often arguing against.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong impression
misattribution.intro: Nobody has stolen this one from Dostoevsky. What travels badly is everything around it — who is speaking, how the sentence ends, and whose English it is.

items.who: Dostoevsky, quoted as if it were his own creed
items.why: The sentence is not narration or authorial commentary. It is read aloud by Ippolit Terentyev from a manuscript headed “An Essential Explanation,” in Part III, Chapter V of the Garnett translation ↗ — a chapter that opens with Ippolit waking on a sofa and breaks off mid-manuscript, on “However, I will continue.” The reading runs straight on through Chapter VI, and the company only turns on him in Chapter VII.

Garnett’s sentence does not end at “the everlasting process.” The full sourced text ↗ reads “the everlasting and perpetual process, not the discovery itself, at all.” In fairness to the aggregators, Wikiquote, Goodreads and Quotefancy all carry that fuller wording; the shortenings we could find drop only “and perpetual” and keep the closing clause.

The quotable rhythm belongs to Constance Garnett. Eva Martin’s translation of the same passage ↗ gives “The important thing is life—life and nothing else! What is any ‘discovery’ whatever compared with the incessant, eternal discovery of life?”

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution holds — it is Dostoevsky’s novel, on a page you can read ↗. It is the framing that gets lost: a dying eighteen-year-old says it, in Garnett’s English, in a sentence one clause longer than the one you have seen.

context.heading: Why a dying boy is talking about Columbus
lead: The line is the climax of one of the strangest set-pieces in Dostoevsky. Ippolit Terentyev, eighteen and dying of consumption, has insisted on reading a long manuscript aloud to a company gathered at Prince Myshkin’s villa. He heads it “An Essential Explanation” and opens with the epigraph Après moi le déluge! He coughs, loses his voice, and keeps going.

The Columbus passage is his answer to a question he throws at his listeners: what do you actually mean by happiness? His claim is that Columbus was happiest three days before land was sighted, with a mutinous crew begging to turn back — because arrival is not the point. Coming from a boy with weeks to live, it is not a motivational poster. It is an argument that a life with no destination left can still be worth having.
context.detailsSummary: What the short form leaves out
detailsBody: Garnett’s sentence does not stop at “the everlasting process.” It reads: “It’s life that matters, nothing but life—the process of discovering, the everlasting and perpetual process, not the discovery itself, at all.” Clipping it there loses both the doubled adjective and the closing clause that actually names what is being rejected.

The English is also very much Garnett’s. Eva Martin’s translation of the same Russian gives the reader a different sentence entirely — “The important thing is life—life and nothing else!” — followed by a question rather than a list. Quoting the line is quoting a translator as well as a novelist.
context.pull: The New World is beside the point. Columbus “died almost without seeing it.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the quotation in its sourced section under The Idiot (1868–9), Part 3, Chapter 5, tr. Constance Garnett, 1913, in the fuller form ending 'not the discovery itself, at all.'

The Constance Garnett translation of The Idiot printed by William Heinemann, London, 1918 contains the exact sentence 'It's life that matters, nothing but life—the process of discovering, the everlasting and perpetual process, not the discovery itself, at all' on page 328, within Part III, Chapter V, in Ippolit Terentyev's manuscript headed 'An Essential Explanation' with the epigraph 'Après moi le déluge!'

Full text of that Heinemann 1918 Garnett printing, showing the title page 'FROM THE RUSSIAN BY CONSTANCE GARNETT / LONDON / WILLIAM HEINEMANN / 1918', the page-328 marker immediately before 'Columbus died almost without seeing it', and Part III Chapter V opening with Ippolit.

Project Gutenberg ebook #2638 is The Idiot translated by Eva Martin, and renders the same passage as 'The important thing is life—life and nothing else! What is any "discovery" whatever compared with the incessant, eternal discovery of life?'
The Idiot was first published serially in The Russian Messenger during 1868–1869, and Constance Garnett's English translation is dated 1913.
Constance Garnett lived 1861–1946 and her translation of Dostoevsky's The Idiot was published in 1913.
Fyodor Dostoevsky was born 11 November 1821 and died 9 February 1881; he was a Russian novelist, essayist and journalist, and The Idiot is dated 1868–1869.
